title: A Snapshot of Influence: A Local Data Attribution Framework for Online Rei

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract says IIF 'completely eliminates sample inefficiency, achieves unprecedented training speed, and solves the long-standing challenge of training instability in online RL'. The reported results in Section 5.2 and Figure 6 show only 20-67% reductions in training rounds and still show learning curves; no evidence supports complete elimination of sample inefficiency or solving training instability.

f^{return}(theta) is defined as E[log pi_theta(a|s) * (-A^{ref}(s,a))]. The text states that maximizing it encourages increasing the probability of better-than-average actions (positive advantage) and decreasing worse-than-average actions. Because of the negative sign, maximizing this objective decreases log pi for positive-advantage actions and increases it for negative-advantage actions, which is the opposite of the stated intent. The later f^{seq} in Section 5.3 uses positive advantage, confirming the sign inconsistency.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, paragraph on reference policy pi^{ref}
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper says pi^{ref} is 'a fixed, pre-trained policy that has been trained to convergence', but then says the 'dynamic reference evolves with training' and that the buffer B^{(k)} collected under pi_{theta^(k)} can be used as the validation set. A fixed pre-trained policy does not evolve and is not the same distribution as the current rollout buffer; these statements contradict each other.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 1 (Introduction), citation 'Kumar et al. [2024]' and References
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Introduction credits 'Kumar et al. [2024]' with demonstrating that data attribution methods can be directly applied to online RL, but no Kumar et al. 2024 entry appears in the reference list. The claim is unverifiable and conflicts with the paper's own assertion of being the first comprehensive study of data attribution for online RL.

The equation for I_i uses the target gradient evaluated at theta_0^{(k)} but the PPO-loss gradient evaluated at theta_j^{(k)}. Section 5.1 later states that the implementation uses <grad f(theta^{(k)}), grad L(theta^{(k)}, z_i)> with both gradients at the initial parameters. This is internally inconsistent and also deviates from the TracIn definition given earlier, where both gradients are evaluated at the same theta_j.

The text reports 'a 20-67% reduction in training rounds required to match the standard training performance', but Figure 6(b) gives SE_ave values from 38.4% to 78.5% and SE_peak values from 28.7% to 82.3%. The stated interval is inconsistent with the paper's own results table.

RT_peak values conflict between Figure 6(b) and Table 5: FrozenLake 38.9 +/- 2.1 vs 31.27 +/- 3.28; Acrobot 67.8 +/- 0.8 vs 55.16 +/- 1.04; MiniGrid 81.7 +/- 1.2 vs 71.59 +/- 1.05; Highway 72.3 +/- 0.9 vs 59.89 +/- 0.72; LunarLander 58.6 +/- 1.8 vs 44.11 +/- 2.29; BipedalWalker 42.1 +/- 0.9 vs 29.16 +/- 0.66. These are the same metric and cannot both be correct.

With n_steps=2048, 1,024,000 timesteps equals 500 rounds, not the stated 1000 rounds for BipedalWalker. Additionally, Appendix B.9 runtimes are inconsistent with stated round counts and per-round runtimes: for MiniGrid, per-round IIF cost is about 4.77 s and 40 rounds would be about 191 s, but Table 5 reports 365 s for all rounds.

B.7 says 'Our main experiments in traditional RL environments are conducted using the SGD optimizer', but A.2 specifies Adam for BipedalWalker and the RLHF experiments use Adam. Section 7 also claims 'we employ SGD as a proxy for Adam', contradicting the actual experimental protocol.

Section 4.1 says it approximates the true advantage using 'Monte Carlo (MC) rollouts from each (s,a), averaging over multiple trajectories', but Appendix B.4 says it computes A-bar from the already-collected rollout buffer 'instead of performing additional sampling'. The main-text description misrepresents the method actually used.

The caption states 'y-axis ranges are optimized to highlight the superior performance of our method' and omits early Acrobot rounds. This is an explicit axis/range selection intended to exaggerate the apparent improvement and can mislead readers about the magnitude of the gains.

IIF's filtering percentage p is selected per environment by evaluating performance ('we evaluate various p's and report the best in Fig. 6'), while the baselines are described as using 'fixed, untuned hyperparameters'. This is a tuned-versus-untuned comparison and does not isolate whether IIF's advantage comes from the attribution method or from per-environment hyperparameter selection.
